demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette:
Robert had always considered his hands to be steady. For forty years as a bank teller, they had counted currency with a crisp, confident rhythm. They had built bookshelves, repaired leaky faucets, and, most importantly, they had held his grandson. That was the memory that now tormented him. The accident had happened six months ago, on a Saturday that was supposed to be perfect. He was at his son’s house, helping to build a small deck in the backyard. The circular saw whined in the afternoon sun, and Robert was focused, measuring a cut. He never heard his grandson, Leo, run up behind him. The first thing he felt was the small, enthusiastic bump against his back, a child’s hug in motion. Startled, Robert lurched, and the saw kicked. The next few seconds unfolded in a silent, horrifying slow motion in his mind: the high-pitched scream, the impossible splash of red on Leo’s jacket, the sight of his own hands, the ones that were supposed to be steady, covered in his grandson’s blood.

Now, those hands tremble. At work, Robert positions his chair tightly against the back of his teller station, a small fortress so that no one can approach from behind. An unexpected touch is unbearable. Last week, a regular customer, Mrs. Gable, reached over the counter to tap his hand affectionately, and he flinched so violently he knocked over his coin tray. The cascade of metal on the floor sounded like a siren in his ears. In that moment, he wasn't in the bank; he was back in the yard, the smell of sawdust and copper in the air. A fragment of the memory, Leo's face contorted in pain, flashed behind his eyes and was gone, leaving him breathless and dizzy. When he remembers the event, the same sickening terror he felt in that instant washes over him, a cold wave that starts in his stomach and leaves him shaking. Immediately following the fear is a crushing, suffocating guilt. He believes he is fundamentally inadequate, a man who failed in his most basic duty to protect his family.

His life has shrunk into a series of defensive maneuvers. He avoids his son’s calls, the cheerful ringtone of his phone now a source of dread. He hasn’t seen Leo since the boy came home from the hospital, his arm wrapped in thick bandages. The thought of seeing the scar, a permanent testament to his failure, is more than he can stand. His son and daughter-in-law insist they don’t blame him, that it was a terrible accident, but their words are meaningless to him. How could they not blame him? He blames himself enough for everyone. This conviction, that his reactions prove he is a lousy coper, has become a core belief. A real man, he thinks, would have faced his family, would have been there for his grandson. Instead, he hides.

The world outside his carefully controlled teller station feels fraught with peril. He is constantly on guard, his body rigid with a tension that never subsides. Even at home, in his favourite armchair, he cannot relax. While his wife watches television, he finds himself scanning the room, listening to the house settle, his heart pounding at every floorboard creak. Sleep offers no escape. He lies awake for hours, certain that he must remain alert, though he doesn't know for what. He feels as though some unseen threat is perpetually waiting, and if he lets his guard down, it will strike. He has come to believe that the cheerful, easygoing man his wife married is gone forever, replaced by this hollow, fearful shell. He feels he has been permanently changed for the worse, and this new version of himself is all he has left. It was after he found himself awake for the third straight night, staring at the ceiling and replaying the saw's screech in his mind, that his wife found him weeping in the kitchen. The next morning, she made the appointment. Robert agreed to come, not with hope, but with a profound fear that the therapist would only confirm what he already knew: that he was broken beyond repair.
